decks.title: Exception Handling — Part 1: Errors, Exceptions, raise and assert
goals: Distinguish syntax errors, exceptions and logical errors
Identify the common built-in exceptions from code and from an error line
Raise exceptions deliberately with raise and check conditions with assert

slides.heading: Exception Handling
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what goes wrong in programs: **syntax errors**, **exceptions**, the **built-in exceptions**, and how to signal problems with **raise** and **assert**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: kinds of errors, syntax errors, exceptions, built-in exceptions, the raise statement and the assert statement
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every programmer meets errors. A good program does not simply crash when something unexpected happens, such as a user typing letters where a number was expected. In this chapter we learn what exceptions are and how Python lets us handle them. Part one looks at the kinds of errors, the common built-in exceptions, and how to raise exceptions ourselves.

slides.heading: Three kinds of errors

rows: While Python parses the program, before it runs
Program runs but prints a wrong answer (`Area: 26`)

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of errors: a syntax error is found while parsing and nothing runs; an exception occurs while the program runs, such as division by zero; a logical error gives a wrong answer without any message
visual.caption: Exception handling deals with the middle row.

slides.narration: Errors come in three kinds. A syntax error breaks the grammar of Python, and it is caught before the program even starts. An exception happens while a correct program is running, for example dividing by zero. A logical error gives no message at all; the program runs but the answer is wrong, as in this area calculation. Exception handling is about the middle kind.

slides.heading: Syntax errors
slides.body_md:
A missing colon is a grammar mistake:

```python
marks = 82
if marks >= 33
    print("Pass")
```

Python reports `SyntaxError: expected ':'` and runs **no** statement, not even the first one.
slides.narration: Here the if statement is missing its colon. Python reads the whole program first, and because the grammar is broken it refuses to run anything at all, not even the first line. That is why a syntax error cannot be caught by a try statement in the same program: the try statement itself never gets to run.

slides.heading: Parse first, then run

nodes.label: Grammar broken? SyntaxError: no statement runs
Grammar fine: statements run one by one
A statement fails at run time: an exception is raised
Handled by try-except, or the program stops with a traceback

visual.alt: Flow: Python first parses the whole program; a broken grammar gives a SyntaxError and nothing runs; otherwise statements run one by one; a failing statement raises an exception, which is either handled by try-except or stops the program with a traceback
visual.caption: Syntax errors stop the program before it starts.

slides.narration: This flow shows what Python does with your program. First it parses the whole file. If the grammar is broken, you get a syntax error and nothing runs. If the grammar is fine, the statements run one by one. When a statement fails while running, Python raises an exception. Either your program handles it, or the program stops and prints a traceback.

slides.body_md: Which exception does the code raise?
slides.narration: Look at the types of the two values being joined by the plus sign.

slides.heading: Reading an error message
slides.body_md:
```python

print("Start")
print(prices[2])
print("End")
```

rows: Exception name (the class of the error)

visual.alt: Table reading an error: the program printed Start, then indexing position 2 of a two-item list raised IndexError with the message list index out of range, so the last print statement never ran
visual.caption: The last line of a traceback names the exception and gives a message.

slides.narration: When an exception is not handled, Python prints a traceback. Its last line is the most useful: it gives the name of the exception, a colon, and a message with details. Here the program printed Start, then asked for position two of a list that has only two items, so Python raised an index error. The final print statement was never reached.

slides.heading: Common built-in exceptions

rows: `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '7k'`
`TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str`
`ZeroDivisionError: integer division or modulo by zero`

visual.alt: Table of six common built-in exceptions, each produced by running the statement in Python: ValueError, TypeError, NameError, IndexError, KeyError and ZeroDivisionError, with their causes

slides.narration: Python has many built-in exceptions, each a class with a name that describes the problem. A value error means the type is right but the value is unsuitable. A type error means the operation does not suit the type. A name error means a variable was never created. Index error and key error are about missing positions and missing keys, and zero division error is about dividing by zero.

slides.heading: More built-in exceptions

rows: file not found (an OSError, also called IOError)
input ended before a line was read

visual.alt: Table of four more built-in exceptions, each produced by running the statement in Python: FileNotFoundError for a missing file, ModuleNotFoundError for a missing module, OverflowError for a result too large, and EOFError when input ends
visual.caption: IOError is another name for OSError in Python 3.

slides.narration: Four more appear in the syllabus. Opening a file that does not exist raises file not found error, a kind of input output error. Importing a module that cannot be found raises an import error. A result too large for a float raises overflow error. And when input runs out before a line is read, Python raises end of file error.

slides.body_md: Which exception is raised?
slides.narration: Compare the name used in the last line with the names that were assigned.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which line fails?
slides.body_md:
Dry-run this program and find where it stops.

```python
stock = {"rice": 40, "dal": 25}
need = "oil"
print("Checking", need)
qty = stock[need]
print("Quantity:", qty)
```

visual.alt: Trace table for a program that looks up oil in a stock dictionary: the first three lines run and print Checking oil, the fourth raises KeyError for oil, and the fifth never runs
visual.caption: Produced by running the program in Python.

slides.narration: Let us dry run this together. Lines one and two create a dictionary and a name. Line three prints Checking oil. Line four looks up oil in the dictionary, but there is no such key, so Python raises a key error and stops. Line five is never reached. In exams, write the output printed before the error and then name the exception.

slides.heading: Raising an exception: raise

nodes.label: Rest of the block is skipped
A matching except handles it (or the program stops)

visual.alt: Flow of raise: the program checks a condition; if the condition is bad it raises a named exception with a message; the rest of the block is skipped; a matching except block handles it, otherwise the program stops
visual.caption: raise throws an exception on purpose.

slides.narration: Sometimes Python sees nothing wrong, but your program knows the data is unacceptable, like a speed above the limit. The raise statement throws an exception on purpose, with a message. The rest of the block is skipped and a matching except block handles it, exactly as if Python had raised it. If no handler matches, the program stops.

slides.heading: Checking assumptions: assert
slides.body_md:
```python
weight = -2
assert weight > 0, "weight must be positive"
```

raises `AssertionError: weight must be positive`

rows: Only if the condition is False
Reject bad data in a finished program

visual.alt: Comparison table of raise and assert: raise throws the named exception every time it runs and is used to reject bad data; assert throws AssertionError only when its condition is False and is used to check assumptions

slides.narration: The assert statement tests a condition. If the condition is true, nothing happens. If it is false, Python raises an assertion error carrying your message. Programmers use assert to check assumptions while developing. Compare it with raise: raise always throws the exception you name, while assert throws only when its condition fails.

bullets: Name the exception **exactly**: `ZeroDivisionError`, not "divide error"; `KeyError` for dictionaries, `IndexError` for lists and strings.

slides.narration: In the exam, write exception names exactly as Python spells them. Remember the classic pairs: converting a decimal string with int is a value error, and joining a string to a number is a type error. In output questions, show what is printed before the failure. A syntax error means nothing is printed at all. And assert only raises when its condition is false.

slides.heading: Handling exceptions
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **try**, **except**, **else** and **finally**, and how to write programs that **recover**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: why handle exceptions, try and except, several except clauses, the order of handlers, else, finally and recovering

slides.narration: In part two we learn to handle exceptions. We will write try and except blocks, use several handlers, see why their order matters, and add else and finally clauses. Then we will write programs that keep asking until the user gives valid input, which is exactly what real applications such as booking counters and fee desks need.

slides.heading: Several except clauses

visual.alt: Table for a loop that floor-divides 100 by the converted value: 4 gives 25 with no exception; 0 raises ZeroDivisionError and its handler runs; four raises ValueError and its handler runs
visual.caption: Each row comes from running the loop in Python.

slides.narration: A try statement can have several except clauses, one for each kind of problem. Python compares the exception with each clause from top to bottom and runs the first one that matches. In this loop, the value four works, zero triggers the zero division handler, and the word four triggers the value error handler.

slides.heading: Grouping and naming exceptions
slides.body_md:
```python
try:
    n = int("12.5")
except (ValueError, TypeError) as e:
    print("Problem:", e)
```

Output: `Problem: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '12.5'`

rows: one handler for either exception (a tuple)
e holds the exception object; `print(e)` shows its message
almost any runtime error (write it last)

visual.alt: Table of except clause forms: one named exception, a tuple of exceptions, the as form that keeps the exception object, the general Exception class written last, and the bare except which should be avoided

slides.narration: You can handle two exceptions with one clause by writing them in a tuple. Adding as, followed by a name, stores the exception object, so you can print its message. The general class Exception catches almost any runtime error, and a bare except catches everything. Use those last two carefully, because they can hide real mistakes.

slides.heading: Order of handlers matters

visual.alt: Table showing that order matters: with the IndexError clause first the index handler runs; with the general Exception clause first, the general handler catches the IndexError and the specific clause is never used
visual.caption: Python runs the first matching clause, top to bottom.

slides.narration: Because Python runs the first matching clause, order matters. In this program the general Exception clause comes first, so it catches the index error, and the specific index handler is never used. Always write specific handlers first and any general handler last.

slides.heading: Quick check: after the handler
slides.body_md: Where does execution continue?
slides.narration: Think about whether Python goes back into the try block after handling an exception.

slides.heading: The else clause

visual.alt: Table of which clauses run: with no exception, else and finally run; with a handled exception, the matching except and finally run; with an unhandled exception only finally runs and then the program stops

slides.narration: An else clause after the except clauses runs only when the try block raised no exception. Put code there that should happen only after the risky step succeeded, like greeting a student once the roll number has been read. This keeps the try block short, so you do not accidentally catch errors from the follow-up code.

slides.heading: The finally clause
slides.body_md:
```python
try:
    print("Lab door opened")
    print(25 / 0)
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Reading failed")
finally:
    print("Lab door locked")
```

Output:

```python
Lab door opened
Reading failed
Lab door locked
```

nodes.label: finally: release it in every case

visual.alt: Flow of the finally pattern: something is opened or reserved, risky work is done in try, an error may be handled or not, and finally releases the resource in every case
visual.caption: Typical uses: closing files and connections, saving logs.

slides.narration: The finally clause runs in every case: after success, after a handled error, and even when an error is not handled or a loop is left with break. That makes it the place for clean-up, such as closing a file or locking the lab door in this example. Notice that the door is locked even though the reading failed.

notes.title: Exception Handling — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Errors and exceptions
sections.body_md:
**Syntax errors** break Python's grammar (missing colon, unmatched bracket, `=` for `==` in a condition). Python finds them while **parsing**, before running, so **no** statement runs and they cannot be handled in the same program.

**Exceptions** (runtime errors) occur while a valid program **runs**, e.g. `10 / 0`. Python creates an exception object and looks for a handler; with none, the program stops and prints a **traceback** whose last line is *ExceptionName: message*.

**Logical errors** give wrong results with no message; only testing reveals them.

sections.heading: 2. Built-in exceptions
sections.body_md:
Each built-in exception is a class named after the problem:

- **ValueError** — right type, unsuitable value: `int("7k")`
- **TypeError** — unsuitable type for an operation: `"Rs " + 50`
- **NameError** — name not defined
- **IndexError** — sequence index out of range
- **KeyError** — dictionary key missing
- **ZeroDivisionError** — divisor zero in `/`, `//` or `%`
- **FileNotFoundError** (an **OSError**, also called **IOError**) — file missing
- **ImportError** (and **ModuleNotFoundError**) — import fails
- **EOFError** — `input()` reaches end of input
- **OverflowError** — result too large
- **SyntaxError** — grammar error

The error lines in the tables were produced by Python 3.12; older versions word some messages slightly differently, but the exception names are the same.

Another name for OSError in Python 3; raised for input-output failures such as a missing file.

```python
except AssertionError as e:

```

sections.heading: 4. try and except
sections.body_md:
Risky statements go in **try**; handlers go in **except** clauses.

- The try block stops at the first failing statement; the rest of it is skipped.
- Python compares the exception with the except clauses **top to bottom** and runs the **first** match; specific handlers first, `except Exception` last.
- `except (ValueError, TypeError):` handles either; `except ValueError as e:` keeps the object, `print(e)` shows the message.
- A bare `except:` catches everything and hides bugs.
- After the handler, execution continues **after** the whole try statement.

sections.heading: 5. else and finally
sections.body_md:
Order: `try`, `except` …, `else`, `finally`.

- **else** runs only if the try block raised **no** exception: use it for work that needs the risky step to succeed.
- **finally** runs in **every** case (success, handled error, unhandled error, `break`): use it for clean-up such as closing files.

```python
try:
    qty = int("3")
except ValueError:
    print("bad")
else:
    print("qty", qty)
finally:
    print("done")
```

Output:

```python
qty 3
done
```

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling `int("4.5")` a TypeError (it is a **ValueError**) or `"5" + 5` a ValueError (it is a **TypeError**).

- Forgetting that **finally** prints in every pass, even after `break`.

- Output questions: each correct line, in the right order.
- Error-finding: the error named **and** corrected.
- Programs: try around the risky step, correct handlers, and output shown for the inputs given.
- Theory: one point per mark, with a short example where it helps.

```python
colours = ["red", "green", "blue"]
```

A delivery app reads a PIN code typed by a user. Which exception is raised here?

```python
pin = int("41a0")
```
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** `ValueError`. int() receives a value of the right type (a string) but with an unsuitable content ("41a0" is not a whole number), so it raises ValueError.

questions.stem_md:
A hostel program joins a label and a room count with the + operator. Which exception is raised?

```python
rooms = 12
print("Rooms: " + rooms)
```
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** `TypeError`. A string cannot be joined to an integer with +; the operand types do not suit the operation, so Python raises TypeError (TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str). Writing str(rooms) fixes it.

Which exception is raised when this code runs?

```python

qty = 3
print(price * qnty)
```
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** `NameError`. qnty is a misspelling of qty and was never assigned, so looking it up raises NameError. The code is syntactically valid, so it is not a syntax error.

A trip planner finds the remainder of the distance by a number of days that is zero. Which exception does this raise?

```python

print(total_km % days)
```
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** `ZeroDivisionError`. The remainder operator, like / and //, cannot use zero as the divisor, so Python raises ZeroDivisionError.

```python
f = open("marks_2026.txt")
```
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** `FileNotFoundError`. Opening a missing file for reading raises FileNotFoundError. It is a kind of OSError, which older programs call IOError (IOError is another name for OSError in Python 3).

questions.stem_md: When is the **finally** block of a try statement executed?

options.text_md: Always, whether or not an exception occurred
Only when the exception was not handled

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Always, whether or not an exception occurred. The finally block runs in every case: after the try block completes, after a handler runs, and even when an unhandled exception is about to stop the program.

questions.stem_md: In a try statement with an **else** clause, when does the else block run?

options.text_md: Only when an exception is raised and handled
Only when the try block finishes without raising an exception
Only when no except clause matches

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Only when the try block finishes without raising an exception. The else block runs only if the try block raised no exception. It is the right place for code that should run only after the risky step succeeded.

questions.stem_md: Which keyword is used to throw an exception deliberately in a Python program?

questions.stem_md: A program has `except ValueError:`, `except ZeroDivisionError:` and `except Exception:` clauses after one try block. Where should `except Exception:` be written, and why?

questions.stem_md: Explain the four clauses of a complete try statement (try, except, else, finally). Describe the order in which they execute when (a) no exception occurs and (b) a handled exception occurs.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each clause and one for the two execution orders.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **try** holds the statements that may raise an exception. It always starts, and it stops at the first statement that fails.
2. **except** (one or more clauses) holds the handler for a named exception. Python checks the clauses from top to bottom and runs only the first one that matches.
3. **else** holds code that should run only if the try block raised **no** exception, such as using a value that was read successfully.
4. **finally** holds clean-up code, such as closing a file, that runs **in every case**, even when the error is not handled.
5. **(a) No exception:** the whole try block → else → finally → the next statement after the try statement. **(b) Handled exception:** the try block up to the failing statement → the matching except block → finally → the next statement; the rest of the try block and the else block are skipped, and the program never returns to the failed line.
